result.markdown: # Vectors & lists ![](/images/Rvector.png){style="width:300px; background: white; border-radius: 5px; border: 5px white solid" fig-align="center"} A __R object__ can hold multiple values. Many __data structures__ can do this with the simplest being a __vector__. A __vector__ can be created with the `c()` __function__. This function will combine the provided objects into a single __vector__ or __list__. __Vectors__ and __lists__ are both 1-dimensional __data structures__. __Vectors__ can only contain one __class__ (homogeneous) whilst __lists__ can contain multiple (heterogeneous). There is more to __lists__ but we will not go into them. ## Creating vector variables ![](/images/list_5.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} Run the following commands to produce __variables__ which contain __vectors__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} number_vec <- c(1,2,4,8,16) number_vec number_series_vec <- 1:6 number_series_vec animals <- c("Whale","Seal","Hedgehog","Mouse","Owl","Squirrel","Vole","Shrew") animals ``` ::: ## Elements and indices ![](/images/index_3.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} Elements of a __vector__ can be accessed through their indices. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Fifth element birds <- animals[5] birds #First to second element aquatic <- animals[1:2] aquatic #Fourth, sixth, and seventh element rodents <- animals[c(4,6,7)] rodents #All except the fifth element mammals <- animals[-5] mammals ``` ::: ## Operators & functions ![](/images/vector_operator.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} You can use __operators__ and __functions__ on a __vector__. When you do each __scalar__ within the __vector__ will be acted upon. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Minus 1 form all element number_vec - 1 #Multiple all elements by 2 number_vec * 2 #Log value of all elements log(number_vec) #The length of vector (i.e. the number of elements) length(rodents) ``` ::: Some __functions__ are specifically used for __vectors__: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(number_vec) summary(number_vec) ``` ::: ## Comparisons ![](/images/comparisons.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} We can also test the values within __vectors__: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Provides vector of logical values for each element aquatic == "Whale" number_vec > 4 #Prints elements with values >4 number_vec[number_vec > 4] ``` ::: ## paste() ![](/images/gluestick.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} The `paste()` __function__ can be used to paste __string scalars__ to other __string scalars__ or to __string vectors__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paste("Animals", animals) bird_or_mammal <- c("mammal","mammal","mammal","mammal","bird","mammal","mammal","mammal") paste(animals, bird_or_mammal, sep = ":") paste(animals, " is a ", bird_or_mammal, sep = "") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
